cards.headline: Cash is harder to fake.
cards.body: Accounting profit bends to judgment calls — depreciation, write-downs, timing. Free cash flow is what actually lands in the bank after running and reinvesting in the business. Valuing a company against its cash, not its reported earnings, sidesteps a lot of the games.

art.name: free-cash-flow
art.alt: Cash from operations, minus capital spending, leaving free cash flow available to the owners.

cards.headline: Price to free cash flow.
cards.body: **Price-to-free-cash-flow** is market cap divided by annual free cash flow — how many dollars you pay for each dollar of real cash the business throws off. It shines when big non-cash charges have dented reported net income.

cards.headline: Flip it into a yield.
cards.body: Turn the ratio upside down and you get a **yield**. Free-cash-flow yield is FCF divided by market cap: **$500M** on a **$10B** company is **5%**. Earnings yield does the same with profit — the inverse of P/E — so a P/E of 20 is a 5% earnings yield.

cards.title: Higher yield, cheaper price?
cards.caption: A higher yield can mean a cheaper price — but only if that cash flow is durable, not a one-year spike.

cards.prompt: A stock's free-cash-flow yield is a fat 9%. Automatically a bargain?

options.label: Only if the cash flow lasts

cards.explanation: A high yield built on a one-off asset sale or a peak year evaporates. Check that the cash flow is repeatable before treating the yield as cheap.

cards.headline: Can the dividend survive?
cards.body: Dividends are paid in cash, so measure them against cash. The **free-cash-flow payout ratio** — dividends divided by FCF — shows the true strain. A dividend swallowing nearly all free cash, or funded by new debt, is a cut waiting to happen.

art.name: payout-pressure
art.alt: A dividend payment consuming most of a company's free cash flow, leaving little room to spare.

cards.body: Because dividends are paid in cash, the [[1]] payout ratio judges their safety better than one based on accounting profit.
cards.explanation: Earnings can show a profit while cash is tight. Since dividends must be paid with real cash, comparing them to free cash flow reveals whether they're truly affordable.

cards.body: A big yield is a question, not an answer. Ask what's behind it before trusting it.

cards.summary: Valuing a company against its cash cuts through accounting noise.
bullets: P/FCF and FCF yield price the real cash a business makes.
A high yield only counts if the cash flow is durable.
Judge dividend safety by the free-cash-flow payout ratio.

art.name: yield-trap
art.alt: An attractively high yield luring an investor toward a payout the company cannot sustain.

cards.insight: A yield is only as safe as the cash behind it. Chase the number without the cash and you inherit the cut.
